title: The fringe and the woven field

object.title: Wrapper (Lamba Akotifahana)
object.observation: The museum records silk, weft-float motifs and rows of knotted fringe. Its account compares the fringe with Chinese-made shawls.
object.limit: That comparison concerns the fringe. The catalogue keeps the place of weaving with the Merina Kingdom.
object.alt: Light silk wrapper with a fine patterned centre, several edge stripes and a pale fringe.

task: Odal is hanging two practice swatches. One tests the field. The other shows why a loose decorative edge needs a separate support.
notes: The model field stays close to the starting span.
The loose practice edge moves farther under the same pull.
choices: Clip the field flat for the Council Yard
Send a slack-edge support to the Lower Channel
responses: The keeper measures the field from the first mark. The edge folds around a free support.
The lower crew hangs the swatch without tension on the fringe. A long tab keeps the fringe comparison with the record.
returnAction: Set a free edge clip beside the fixed field
returnEffect: A visitor can distinguish the supported field from the loose fringe. The reference still credits a Merina weaver.

title: Where the panels meet

object.title: Woman's Skirt
object.medium: Raffia palm fiber (Raphia ruffia or R. vinifera) and dye
object.observation: The catalogue describes floated weft patterns inside the panels and extra short tufts crossing the seams of the raffia skirt.
object.limit: The catalogue describes the construction and design of this skirt. The practice strips use plain seam markers.
object.alt: Antique raffia skirt laid flat, with a pale centre, darker borders and a central seam.

task: Odal has two identical-looking sides on the practice frame. An extra join crosses one pull.
notes: The ends stay on the same straight thread.
The join draws out an extra stretch in this practice strip.
choices: Keep the panel in view at the Yard
Put the seam reading on the Lower Channel sleeve
responses: The Yard copy gives the main panel room to lie flat. A side slip points to the seam in the catalogue.
The next carrier opens the sleeve at the seam. A short note credits the work of weavers and embroiderers separately.
returnAction: Lift the false edge and clip the seam where the tufts cross
returnEffect: The display line now names the join before it names the fabric edge. A visitor can use both notes.

title: A tied patch takes a different load

object.title: Man's Garment
object.medium: Raffia palm fiber (Raphia ruffia or R. vinifera) and dye
object.observation: The museum describes a raffia wrapper with knot-and-twist resist dyeing. Tying helps account for the crinkled surface.
object.limit: A flat photograph shows the pattern well. Material behaviour in the practice clip belongs to our plain swatches.
object.alt: Raffia garment with a red and ochre repeating pattern and short brown fringe.

task: A small carrier wants to fold a copy into a sleeve. Odal keeps a loose strip beside a creased practice section so both can be tried.
checks: Pull across the tied practice fold
notes: The plain strip changes a little.
The fold opens first, giving this strip more travel under tension.
choices: Keep one loose plane visible in the Yard
Send the fold-and-open sequence to the channel
responses: A Yard reader can point to the flat pattern and read separately why the fibre looks crinkled.
A carrier sees one strip opening before it takes more load. The proof names the actual Dida-style technique with its source.
returnAction: Clip a fold tab over the old smooth-surface heading
returnEffect: The shelf now shows that a pattern and a small raised fold need different observations.

title: The six joined strips

object.title: Blanket or Cover (Kaasa)
object.origin: Mali, Niger or Burkina Faso, with a Fulani attribution
object.observation: The catalogue describes a wool cover made from six handwoven strips joined along their selvages.
object.limit: The listed geography is broad. The shared textile description gives no single place of manufacture for this cover.
object.alt: Wool blanket with tall bands of dark repeating shapes and dark red edges.

task: Odal wants the working copy to make the count of six visible even when the sample covers several joins.
checks: Pull across the mock selvage join
notes: The first pull follows one plain strip.
The second pull makes a join spread across the two clips.
choices: Unroll the full six-strip count in the Yard
Send a folded sleeve with edge tabs for the seams
responses: The Yard keeper traces five meets between the six strips. They leave the broad location on the source slip.
A lower handler unfolds each tab at a join and can rebuild the count even from the compact sheet.
returnAction: Replace the “one piece” tab with a six-strip count
returnEffect: The old heading stays readable underneath. The shelf now shows how the six-strip count was reached.

title: Two faces from one hanging

object.title: Wall Hanging (msimsim)
object.observation: The museum describes a silk brocade grid with navy and crimson faces and connects msimsim hangings to recorded marriage gifts in Tétouan.
object.limit: The source allows two possible supplies for the raw silk. It identifies neither a particular loom nor this hanging’s silk supplier.
object.alt: A long hanging with one dense patterned field between dark outer borders.

task: Odal needs two support notes for one practice plane. A folded corner hides the far face from a viewer in the line.
notes: The colour-facing plane stays close to the first span.
The fold opens in larger motion before the opposite face lies flat.
choices: Show one face with a turn tab in the Yard
Send a two-sided handling clip to the channel
responses: A viewer can find the note for the unseen face without turning the copy. The geographic label says Tétouan.
A channel reader turns the clipped sheet and sees where the two documented colour faces are labelled.
returnAction: Fit a turn tab so both brocade faces stay labelled
returnEffect: A reader can turn the sheet without confusing the craft location with the silk’s possible origins.

title: A joining ribbon and a missing width

object.title: Curtain panel (sitara)
object.observation: The museum describes an Algerian curtain with two surviving embroidered widths and joined ribbons. It says a third width is missing.
object.limit: The catalogue describes the original layout from comparable curtains. The missing width itself is absent.
object.alt: A narrow curtain panel with vertical embroidered borders and coloured joining ribbons.

task: An old clipping shows the surviving cloth and leaves no space for the third width. Odal wants the two lengths to stay legible during handling.
notes: The ground stays closer to its unloaded span.
The fixture adds travel at the mock joining ribbon.
choices: Hang the narrow copy and label the surviving edges
Give the channel reader a fold for the missing width
responses: The narrow copy shows two widths. A plain marker says a third is described in the source.
The sleeve unfolds into two occupied columns and an empty third. A carrier can distinguish estimate and surviving fabric.
returnAction: Open a slot beside the two surviving widths
returnEffect: A viewer can now see the gap without seeing a coloured replacement for it. The source stays clipped to both references.

title: Two curtains and one mount

object.title: Curtain
object.observation: The Cleveland record groups two curtains. It records silk bands, gold embroidery and how weaving and embroidery were distinct jobs.
object.limit: The account describes possible household and special-occasion uses. This particular pair’s original room is unrecorded.
object.alt: Two striped curtains in the same photograph, each with multicoloured narrow bands.

task: Odal has to hang a pair without making a false join between the two curtain lengths.
checks: Grip across a paper installation joint
notes: The band moves under one set of marks.
The fixture’s installation joint opens farther.
choices: Show the two lengths on separate Yard clips
Keep the two lengths together with a divider at the channel
responses: Each hanging has its own hook and both still share the catalogue entry.
A divider lets a lower handler interpret both curtains as one catalogue pair and still locate each edge.
returnAction: Unclip the false seam between the two mounts
returnEffect: The label keeps two original lengths and one catalogue entry. The hanging room remains open in the record.

title: The fall at the end of a scarf

object.title: Scarf End
object.observation: The Met catalogues this late eighteenth-century wool piece as a scarf end, 24.1 by 76.2 centimetres.
object.limit: Its measured size belongs to the surviving end. The whole scarf’s length is open.
object.alt: A pale and red piece of wool with two visible tassels at its lower edge.

task: The first tray grips the broad strip. A second holder lets the small tassels hang past the edge.
checks: Clamp across the mock tassel row
notes: The straight strip stretches less.
The separated mock ends add more travel.
choices: Lay the complete surviving end flat in the Yard
Roll the loose ends around a separate channel sleeve
responses: The measurable edge is clear. A Yard reader can check the recorded size without assuming a complete scarf.
The sleeves keep the little ends intact. A stop tab points to the measurement of this fragment.
returnAction: Move the length line to the surviving end
returnEffect: A reader can tell which distance has a source. The proposed full length remains blank.

title: A joined damask hanging

object.title: Hanging
object.observation: The Met lists joined damask silk and records the whole hanging at 217.2 by 173.4 centimetres.
object.limit: The Attributed to Tunisia wording expresses a geographical attribution. This record does not provide a named workshop.
object.alt: Red hanging with two large patterned panels and a narrow joining line.

task: A straight clamp shows one panel. A second clamp crosses the join so the room can decide where to put a support.
notes: The model panel takes the marked load.
The seam strip lengthens more at the same mark.
choices: Mount one panel view and a joint line in the Yard
Put two joined leaves in the channel holder
responses: A first viewer can recognise the join before tracing the full width. The label preserves the attribution.
The lower receiver unfolds both leaves. The support sits under the join and the catalogue’s stated overall width stays on the slip.
returnAction: Move the bearing clip beneath the joined section
returnEffect: The public copy now preserves two support points and the cautious geographical attribution.

title: The grip on a round jar

object.title: Water Transport Jar
object.dimensions: Diameter: 35.7 cm (14 1/16 in.); Overall: 36.9 cm (14 1/2 in.)
object.observation: The museum describes a female potter joining two clay bowls to form the jar’s body and pressing surface designs to help a person grip it.
object.limit: The source estimates a relationship to gourd shapes. The fixture measures the outline of a fictional load.
object.alt: Round terracotta water jar with a short neck and textured brown surface.

task: An empty hoop leaves room for the grip strip. A broad board gives the practice load more support on an incline.
notes: The plain load line crosses the narrow edge at this incline.
There is still room on the broad board. The textured side mark stays visible.
choices: Show the grip strip on the Yard’s open tray
Send the wider base guide to the lower bank
responses: The keeper points to the pressed section before trying the mock lift. The checked support stays printed on the receipt.
A lower carrier sets out the broader foot line and can see where the two bowl shapes meet.
returnAction: Fit the plain grip strip to the broad support
returnEffect: A carrier can trace the clay join and still distinguish grip from bearing width.

title: The stack without its stopper

object.title: Set of Nesting Wedding Baskets
object.dimensions: Diameter of mouth with rim: 16.6 x 15.2 cm (6 9/16 x 6 in.); Diameter of base: 6.4 x 3.2 cm (2 1/2 x 1 1/4 in.); Part 2: 16.6 x 14 cm (6 9/16 x 5 1/2 in.); Part 3: 13.8 x 12.7 cm (5 7/16 x 5 in.); Part 4: 13.1 x 11.5 cm (5 3/16 x 4 1/2 in.); Part 5: 12.1 x 10.5 cm (4 3/4 x 4 1/8 in.); at mouth: 6.4 x 5.8 cm (2 1/2 x 2 5/16 in.); Across top: 6.8 x 7 cm (2 11/16 x 2 3/4 in.); Body: 5.4 x 4.9 cm (2 1/8 x 1 15/16 in.); Width at top: 10 x 9.3 cm (3 15/16 x 3 11/16 in.); width of mouth: 9.5 x 8.3 cm (3 3/4 x 3 1/4 in.)
object.observation: The catalogue groups ten nesting baskets and a stopper. It gives separate dimensions for the graduated parts.
object.limit: The catalogue identifies the set as wedding baskets. The workshop test compares plain nested trays with their parts stacked.
object.alt: Tapered dark woven stack with a pointed top and horizontal patterning.

task: The Yard keeper wants a quick stack count. Osma kept a separate shelf where each loose ring can be supported.
checks: Set the nested model on one foot
Separate the plain stopper on the wide support
notes: The assembled stack keeps a small edge margin.
The widened support leaves a larger margin for the separated model.
choices: Mount the assembled-stack count in the Yard
Send an exploded parts plan with the stopper’s own tab
responses: The Yard can count one packed set and direct a reader to the ten baskets below it.
A lower handler counts the cloth model’s ten rings and the separate stopper marker before fitting them into one stack.
returnAction: Attach a separate stopper tab above the ten-stack count
returnEffect: The shelf’s receipt now keeps the stopper distinct from the ten baskets.

title: Support for a broad woven top

object.title: Basket
object.dimensions: Overall: 22.5 cm (8 7/8 in.); Diameter of top: 31.6 cm (12 7/16 in.)
object.observation: The record calls this object a basket and measures the top at 31.6 centimetres across. A catalogue note calls it a hat and connects it to visitors passing through Ekibondo.
object.limit: The two terms come from one public catalogue entry. They leave the original use of this particular object open.
object.alt: Wide straight-sided woven form with dark angular patterning and a plain rim.

task: A round outline crosses two supports. The narrower one leaves the rim clear and the wider one changes how far the model can tip.
notes: The rim stays exposed and the load line goes past the edge.
The broad board keeps a margin. The free rim can be marked separately.
choices: Keep the rim visible and both catalogue terms beside it
Send the base board that keeps the open rim marked
responses: A Yard handler can verify the top diameter and read the source’s two terms at the same time.
A lower handler checks the board. A separate tab gives the catalogue title and its alternate wording.
returnAction: Clip both catalogue terms beside the measured rim
returnEffect: The object’s label can keep an observed rim measurement while acknowledging the two different catalogue words.

title: The carrying strap and the belly

object.title: Water Jug and Carrying Strap
object.dimensions: Overall: 64.8 cm (25 1/2 in.); Diameter of mouth with rim: 17.8 x 8.9 cm (7 x 3 1/2 in.)
object.identity: Unidentified maker of the jug and strap
object.observation: The accession groups a terracotta water jug with a separate plant-fibre carrying strap.
object.limit: The record gives material and dimensions. It leaves the makers and the original carrying route open.
object.alt: A round jug with dark neck held in a light woven loop with a strap.

task: The practice jar can sit on its strap or be held by a floor support. Avoid letting the strap sit beneath a measured edge.
checks: Lay the strap under the model
Suspend the strap and rest the belly
notes: The strap shifts the plain load toward the measured edge.
The separate support gives the jug model more room on the tilt.
choices: Keep the strap line visible beside the jug in the Yard
Give the lower crew the belly-support sketch and a separate strap tab
responses: A viewer can follow the strap round the vessel without treating it as the stable stand.
The lower crew fits the support under the belly and traces the strap on another line of the receipt.
returnAction: Hang the strap reference beside the jug rather than under its foot
returnEffect: A handler can read the plant-fibre label without making it cover the stand measurement.

title: A round bottom needs a bearing

object.title: Vase with Small Neck and Round Bottom
object.dimensions: H: 1 5/16 in. (3.35 cm); Top Diam: 3/8 in. (0.97 cm); Base Diam: 1 1/4 in. (3.21 cm)
object.observation: The museum gives separate top and base diameters for the small Egyptian vase and identifies a rounded bottom in the object title.
object.limit: The measurement records this stone form. Its former contents and how it stood in use remain open.
object.alt: Pale stone vase with a narrow neck, rounded body and dark mineral markings.

task: A narrow ring catches the plain model’s curve. An open board leaves the outline readable.
checks: Tilt the model on the open board
Tilt the model in a wide bearing ring
notes: The mock load passes just outside the board’s mark.
The bearing ring leaves another three marks to the edge.
choices: Show the top and base measurements in the Yard
Send a fitted support sketch to the channel
responses: A viewer knows which diameter belongs to the mouth and which is below it.
A lower attendant can seat the rounded practice form safely and preserves each museum measurement on the slip.
returnAction: Set a free cradle tab under the round-bottom sketch
returnEffect: The shelf keeps the help a carrier needs alongside the smaller diameter at the lip.

title: The edge of a small molded lamp

object.title: Lamp
object.observation: The Met records molded earthenware from Utica and lists three dimensions for this lamp.
object.limit: From Utica gives the catalogue geography. It leaves this individual object’s workshop and fuel unrecorded.
object.alt: Reddish earthenware lamp with a projecting spout and several holes.

task: The yard tray should show the spout. A lower carrier wants a deep restraint that keeps a model from sliding forward.
checks: Tilt on a thin rim shelf
Tilt in a broad spout cradle
notes: The projecting end runs past the support mark.
The broad cradle leaves a clear margin around the spout.
choices: Keep the spout view and a rim caution in the Yard
Give the channel the model cradle sketch
responses: The first visitor can identify the spout. A separate line marks why the narrow support was unsuitable in the model.
The lower attendant sets the longer support before the lip and keeps the Utica attribution in view.
returnAction: Move the spout support line beyond the rim
returnEffect: The reading stand now keeps the spout’s shape visible and gives the next handler the bearing mark.

title: A long tube across one support

object.title: Marovany
object.observation: The Met catalogues a bamboo-and-wood marovany, 124.5 centimetres long and 7.6 centimetres across.
object.limit: The catalogue fixes dimensions and materials. It supplies no measurement of playing tension for this individual object.
object.alt: Long, narrow bamboo instrument photographed side-on with a few small surface details.

task: A long model tube can rest on one clip or split its load between two clips. Keep the width of the tube visible on the sheet.
notes: The mock load passes the single clip’s mark.
Two spots keep the practice tube inside the rated edge.
choices: Keep the long silhouette across the open Yard board
Send the paired bearing points to the lower bank
responses: A Yard reader can see how far the narrow tube extends past the first support.
The lower carrier aligns the two bearing marks while leaving the museum’s separate length and diameter visible.
returnAction: Clip the second support mark at the far end of the silhouette
returnEffect: The shelf records two physical support points and keeps the reported span separate from the fictional handling trial.

title: A water jug lying across its handles

object.title: Barrel Jug with Geometric Decoration
object.observation: The Walters describes an Iron Age water jug whose body resembles a barrel lying on its side.
object.limit: The catalogue supplies the form and later estate gift. The route travelled by the jug in antiquity is open.
object.alt: Ceramic barrel-shaped jug with a short neck, small handle and visible concentric bands.

task: Osma has a flat support and a wider curved block. The object’s sideways form presents a bearing direction that a normal vertical bottle would not.
checks: Tilt the model on the flat runner
Tilt the model in the side cradle
notes: The round model runs beyond the marked flat edge.
The side cradle leaves three marks inside its edge.
choices: Publish a side profile with the bearing caution
Send the side cradle guide to the Lower Channel
responses: The Yard holder learns why the short neck does not determine the jug’s load direction.
A lower handler uses the wider cradle. Its label points to the precise Cypriot jug form.
returnAction: Move the directional arrow along the barrel’s side
returnEffect: The two arrows now distinguish the mouth direction from the resting direction.

title: The handle stops at the rim

object.title: Handle with the Head of a Woman
object.observation: The Walters identifies this bronze piece as an attachment where the handle met the rim of a water jug.
object.limit: The surviving part contains a handle attachment. The shape and load of the whole historic jug are open.
object.alt: A dark bronze fragment with a small face at the top and curved projections.

task: A plain handle model shifts on its own. A separate rim support shows how the ends might have met.
checks: Tilt the handle model by itself
Tilt the model against the rim block
notes: The isolated handle crosses the marked edge.
The second support shows the practice attachment bearing in two places.
choices: Keep the fragment’s outer contour open in the Yard
Send the possible attachment line on a separate sleeve
responses: A Yard visitor can point to the surviving bronze and see an open line where the rest is missing.
A lower handler sees where a rim could take the plain model’s load and where the historical fragment ends.
returnAction: Set a seam tab where the handle could meet a rim
returnEffect: The source distinction between attachment and whole jug stays visible after the shelf closes.

title: Who a stamped weight names

object.title: Inscribed Pound Weight
object.origin: Damascus is the recorded discovery place
object.observation: The Walters describes this green glass weight as stamped and names Yazid III in its inscription. It lists al-Walid ibn Abdul-Rahman as patron.
object.limit: The catalogue puts discovery in Damascus. The discovery line and named roles give separate information.
object.alt: Round green glass weight with a darker recessed edge and stamped centre.
object.dateKind: Dated inscription in the Walters record

task: A clerk can follow a fast name index or a longer docket that reaches the find-place drawer. Keep patron, inscription and discovery on their own slips.
notes: This index reaches the named inscription and patron fields.
The second route reaches the accession folder with the Damascus discovery line.
choices: Send the patron and inscription index to the Yard
Send the discovery docket to the Lower Channel
responses: A reader reaches the two names from one index. A place strip remains available behind it.
The lower reader can show exactly which line says Damascus and which line states the catalogue date.
returnAction: Keep the patron and find-place under separate clips
returnEffect: The Canal index can now take readers to the name record or the discovery note. Each remains available.

title: Two possible origin lines

object.title: Aquamanile (Handwasher) in the Form of a Cheetah
object.origin: Egypt or Italy, both qualified in the source
object.identity: Unidentified maker, with Egyptian and Italian attributions considered
object.observation: The Walters identifies an animal-shaped bronze pouring vessel and keeps Egyptian and Italian maker attributions open.
object.limit: The wider catalogue compares animal bronzes across several sites. The precise place of making for this particular vessel remains open.
object.alt: A dark bronze cheetah-shaped container with four legs, a loop handle and a projecting mouth.

task: The Yard needs a form tag. A channel reader tracing the longer docket needs to read both possible origins without treating either as a routing command.
notes: The outer shape and title can be found quickly.
This route retains both possible origins and their question marks.
choices: Show the pouring form with one locator tab
Send the folded two-origin docket to the channel
responses: A visitor finds the physical form and a side tab gives the two possible origins.
A lower reader opens the separate attribution fields and keeps both in the public copy.
returnAction: Pin the two provisional origins side by side
returnEffect: Neither place has become the main heading. An open copy links to why the museum compares both.

title: One earring, two attributions

object.title: Earring
object.origin: Syria or Egypt, both qualified in the source
object.observation: The Walters lists granulated gold and two possible places for this earring. It separately records Henry Walters’s purchase in 1913.
object.limit: The purchase date traces custody. The catalogue leaves the place of manufacture open.
object.alt: Fine wire loop above a clustered gold ornament, photographed against black.

task: A small case card needs a short route to the goldwork. A second clerk needs a longer docket to separate the purchase from the possible origins.
checks: Carry the medium slip through the fast rail
Carry the acquisition line and both possible origins
notes: The fast rail finds the granulation note.
The side rail collects the attributed origins and a distinct purchase stamp.
choices: Keep the granulated-gold line at the Yard’s open tray
Send the purchase and both maker-attribution lines to the channel
responses: The first reader locates the metalwork. The label preserves both possible origins in a separate place.
The lower keeper can locate 1913 without converting it into the making date.
returnAction: Separate the purchase clip from the two-origin card
returnEffect: Canal visitors can follow the custody note independently of the attribution.

title: The later repair and the original comb

object.title: Comb with Scrolls and Birds
object.identity: Unidentified Sicilian maker and later repairer
object.observation: The Walters describes an ivory comb with two decorated faces, later repaired across the break. Many teeth are missing.
object.limit: The catalogue leaves the date and maker of the repair open. The Sicilian attribution belongs to the comb.
object.alt: A rectangular comb with a round design in the middle, gaps in the teeth and an obvious break through the centre.

task: Two rails carry a usable form card and a longer conservation docket. The visitor wants to know why some teeth are missing.
notes: The short route finds the shape, two faces and lost teeth.
The longer docket marks the repair as a separate event with no date supplied.
choices: Keep a two-sided shape copy in the Yard
Send the repair and later custody separately to the channel
responses: A visitor turns the paper and can find the missing teeth in the outline view.
A lower keeper can point to the repaired junction while preserving the recorded 1930 purchase.
returnAction: Clip the later repair above the making date line
returnEffect: The marked break stays distinct from the catalogue date of the comb and from the recorded 1930 purchase.

title: A jug whose catalogue lists several places

object.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art
object.title: Bartmann jug
object.origin: Germany, Democratic Republic of the Congo and Congo appear in the geography field
object.observation: The Smithsonian describes a salt-glazed Bartmann jug with a bearded face and gives the Walshaert collection in Antwerp before 1930 in the provenance.
object.limit: The record links the form with German pottery. The geography field leaves the sequence of travel for this particular jug open.
object.alt: Tall brown glazed jug with a narrow neck and an outline of a handle.

task: The geography list resembles a travel line. Test a short type card and a longer route docket that has spaces for unknown handovers.
checks: Take the custody docket to its final stop
notes: The first rail reaches the form label and the salt glaze note.
The longer rail reaches the known Antwerp line with open spaces before it.
choices: Hang the form and glaze identification in the Yard
Put the known Antwerp stop and open spaces in the channel sleeve
responses: The keeper can explain the vessel form without putting the other names in a made-up order.
The lower reader locates the collection history and can mark an uncertain leg as open.
returnAction: Leave a blank between the type origin and Antwerp
returnEffect: The Canal display preserves the exact geography field without converting it into a made-up route.

title: The guild made the plaque

object.title: Plaque with Two Portuguese Merchants
object.observation: The Met credits brass-casting guild artists for the plaque and identifies the depicted figures as Portuguese merchants.
object.limit: The museum distinguishes the people represented, the guild that made the plaque and the modern collection history. It gives no personal names for the merchants.
object.alt: A brown rectangular brass plaque with two standing figures in relief.

task: A visitor copied the depicted figures into the makers line. Taev’s two rails put the artist field and the represented subjects back into separate drawers.
checks: Carry the depicted merchants and provenance docket
notes: The first rail preserves the guild in the maker’s field.
The second rail preserves the subject and collection-history references without assigning either the making role.
choices: Lead with the guild’s name in the Yard
Publish separate maker and represented-person lines by the channel
responses: A reader starts at the guild record and can turn the short slip to find which figures appear.
The lower reader can cite both roles before following the separate museum provenance.
returnAction: Set the guild tab onto the making line
returnEffect: The Canal copy now shows how readers can locate the depicted merchants while keeping credit with the named guild.

title: Two pendants in one accession

object.title: Pendants
object.dimensions: Catalogued height 5 cm and diameter 2 cm for each part
object.observation: The Met records two numbered silver pendants under one accession and retains a probable Moroccan geographical attribution.
object.limit: The catalogue gives individual dimensions for the two parts. It leaves manufacture and original wearer unrecorded at this level.
object.alt: Two similarly shaped dark pendants with pierced upper ends and curved tips.

task: A runner’s slip can give the shared entry. A keeper who rehangs a loose part needs the separate a and b references.
checks: Send both lettered part receipts through the keeper rail
notes: One accession reaches the paired record.
The extra stop can resolve the two lettered parts without assigning a known maker.
choices: Forward the shared locator to the Yard
Leave the two distinct part lines at the lower receiver
responses: The first reader can find the pair immediately and sees the qualifier alongside Morocco.
The lower keeper checks each labelled part against the pair instead of assigning a new accession.
returnAction: Reclip the two part letters underneath their shared accession
returnEffect: Both part records can be opened from one index. The probably line stays in place.

title: A place attribution and a gift stamp

object.title: Nose Ring
object.observation: The Met catalogues a gold nose ring as probably nineteenth century and attributes it to Ethiopia. The credit line names Meredith Howland’s 1904 gift.
object.limit: The date and geography are catalogue attributions. The donor credit does not supply the named maker or an original owner.
object.alt: Small gold-coloured ring with an opening at the bottom.

task: One label fits two lines. Taev will either lead with the attributed date or place the gift and material on separate slips.
checks: Carry the gift receipt and qualify its context
notes: The production-date rail retains “probably.”
The other rail reaches 1904 as the gift date and leaves the maker line open.
choices: Show the working date line with a source in the Yard
Send the gift receipt beside the details to the channel
responses: The first reader can repeat the date as an attribution. The gift is still easy to locate.
The channel copy puts 1904 right beside the gifting role and retains the earlier probable date.
returnAction: Split the gift stamp and date attribution into two pockets
returnEffect: A reader reopening the shelf can find either date and tell which event it describes.

title: A local description in a different department

object.title: Fragment
object.dimensions: L. 10 x W. 1 3/4 inches (25.4 x 4.4 cm)
object.origin: Madagascar in the catalogue culture field
object.observation: The Met lists this as a nineteenth-century bobbin-lace fragment associated with Madagascar. It is filed in European Sculpture and Decorative Arts.
object.limit: The department is a museum filing choice. The accession leaves the original worker, workplace and route to the collection open.
object.alt: Narrow cream lace fragment with repeated curved edges and a small museum measurement tag.

checks: Follow the material route to the narrow lace
Follow the department index to the accession drawer

The longer route shows how the department separates the filing location from the attribution.

Give the lower reader the museum drawer path with both fields
responses: The work stays associated with Madagascar in the open display. A note gives the department for searching.
A carrier finds the institution’s file and can read the cultural context without treating the department as its place of making.
returnAction: Reclip the department name below the collection entry
returnEffect: The shelf now shows an institutional category and the object’s documented cultural field separately.

title: The painted edge in a glancing view

object.medium: earthenware, with luster decoration and glaze
object.observation: The Walters catalogue identifies glazed earthenware with luster decoration and describes yellow-golden painting around a central bird.

Send a glancing check and frame marker to the channel

title: A painted face with no surviving backing

object.observation: The Walters records paint on red-stained parchment or alum-tawed hide. The description leaves a possible book-cover function open because no backing is preserved.

title: A signature beside a worn scene

object.origin: Greece is the recorded discovery place
object.observation: The Walters reads Gnaios’s name on the garnet. The depicted athlete may be based on a work related to Polykleitos. The museum records damage from earlier cleaning.

task: Zyra has a sharp name slip and an eroded model scene. The cover lamp and the side lamp can keep the two observations separate.
notes: The edge view preserves a clear index mark.
The side view shows the patch that hides part of the model figure.

Send the worn-scene comparison to the channel
responses: A reader can locate Gnaios, the inscribed name. The possible model stays on the side note.
The lower viewer sees where wear affects seeing the figure and where the signature was read.
returnAction: Set the worn area beside the signature on different tabs
returnEffect: The corrected shelf distinguishes the named gem carver, the damaged surface and the possible older model.

title: Space between the comb teeth

Keep the tooth and join alongside the protective channel sleeve

title: A shallow spoon with incised lines

object.title: Spoon
